reply: The concept cannot be approved as stated because a visible/NIR silica fiber cannot transmit the mid‑IR wavelengths needed for an ATR measurement of water in oil; a MIR‑transparent fiber or a much shorter link is required.

limitations: Vis-NIR silica fibre carries the MIR (ATR) range: A Vis-NIR silica fibre transmits about 0.35–2.4 µm; MIR (ATR) works at 4000–400 cm⁻¹ (2.5–25 µm). The link cannot carry the signal. Mid-IR fibre link: distance not shown to be feasible: MIR (ATR) needs mid-IR fibres, and the enquiry implies an analyzer away from the line (length not given). risks: Silica fiber will not transmit MIR light, leading to no signal.
Long fiber runs may introduce loss; MIR fibers have higher attenuation than silica.
High temperature/pressure may exceed fiber rating.
Oil opacity or particulates could limit ATR penetration depth.
The mid-IR fibre link over the required distance is not shown to be feasible in the supplied material.

steps: Obtain a small set of oil samples with known water concentrations (lab reference).
Test a short length of MIR‑transparent fiber (e.g., 1 m chalcogenide) between the probe and a bench FTIR to verify transmission.
Measure them with a laboratory FTIR ATR bench to build a calibration model.
Install the probe in a pilot‑scale loop and run the fiber to the remote analyzer; collect spectra and validate against the reference method on held‑out samples.
Evaluate signal‑to‑noise, drift, and robustness under process temperature/pressure.
feasibility.decisionBasis: If step 3 shows acceptable transmission and step 4 validates the calibration on independent samples, the MIR‑ATR concept is feasible; otherwise, revert to NIR transmission using existing silica fiber. Agree two things separately with the customer before the test: the model accuracy required against the reference method, and the alarm or action threshold applied to the measured value.
